$n = 40$

$\sum m = 3404$

$\sum m^{2} = 297  409$

Calculate an unbiased estimate of the population mean mass of a brownie, and show that an unbiased estimate of the population variance is 198, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_md:
To find an unbiased estimate of the population mean, use $\overline{m} = \frac{\summ}{n}$

$\overline{m} = \frac{3404}{40}$

$\overline{m} = 85 . 1$

**[B1]**

To find an unbiased estimate of the population variance, use `s^{2} = \dfrac{1}{n - 1}\left(\sum m^{2} - \dfrac{\left(\sum m\right)^{2}}{n}\right)`

`s^{2} = \dfrac{1}{39}\left(297\,409 - \dfrac{3404^{2}}{40}\right)`

**[M1]**

$s^{2} = \frac{7728.6}{39} = 198 . 169 \dots$

**Final answer:** $s^{2} = 198$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Unbiased estimate of the mean = 85.1.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution into either form of the unbiased variance formula. Use of the biased variance, dividing by 40 instead of 39 (giving 193), scores M0 A0.
> 
> **A1**: 198 correctly obtained, with the unrounded value (198.17 or better) seen before rounding. The answer is given in the question, so the working must be shown.

parts.problem_md:
Sasha takes another random sample of $n$ brownies from ChocoCakes, where $n$ is large, and calculates the sample mean mass, $\overline{M}$ grams. It is given that $\text{P} ( \overline{M} > 81 . 6 ) = 0 . 9909$.

Using your estimates from part (a),

(i) write down the approximate distribution of $\overline{M}$, stating the values of any parameters,

(ii) show that $3 . 5 \sqrt{\frac{n}{198}} = 2 . 36$,

(iii) hence find the value of $n$.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

$n$ is large, so by the Central Limit theorem $\overline{M}$ is approximately normal, with mean 85.1 and variance $\frac{198}{n}$

`\bar{M} \sim \text{N}\left(85.1, \; \dfrac{198}{n}\right)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

0.9909 is more than 0.5, so 81.6 is below the mean and its z-value is negative. 0.9909 is in the table of the normal distribution function in the 2.3 row and 6 column

$Φ ( 2 . 36 ) = 0 . 9909$

$z = - 2 . 36$

**[B1]**

Standardise 81.6 using the formula for the sample mean, with $\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{198}{n}}$

$Z = \frac{\overline{M}-μ}{\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}}$

$\frac{81.6-85.1}{\sqrt{\frac{198}{n}}} = - 2 . 36$

**[M1]**

Dividing by $\sqrt{\frac{198}{n}}$ is the same as multiplying by $\sqrt{\frac{n}{198}}$

$- 3 . 5 \sqrt{\frac{n}{198}} = - 2 . 36$

$3 . 5 \sqrt{\frac{n}{198}} = 2 . 36$

**[A1]**

(iii)

Divide by 3.5, then square both sides

$\sqrt{\frac{n}{198}} = \frac{2.36}{3.5}$

`n = 198 \times \left(\dfrac{2.36}{3.5}\right)^{2} = 90.02\ldots`

$n$ is a sample size, so it is a whole number

$n = 90$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: `\bar{M} \sim \text{N}\left(85.1, \; \dfrac{198}{n}\right)`, or normal with mean 85.1 and variance $\frac{198}{n}$.
> 
> **B1**: z = ±2.36 from $Φ ( z ) = 0 . 9909$.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising 81.6 with 85.1 and $\sqrt{\frac{198}{n}}$, equated to ±2.36.
> 
> **A1**: The given equation obtained with no errors seen. The answer is given in the question, so the steps must be shown.
> 
> **B1**: n = 90. The answer must be a whole number.

parts.problem_md:
The amount of rainfall, $X$ millimetres, on a summer's day in London has mean 1.6 and standard deviation 0.6.

A random sample of 40 summer days is taken. Find the probability that the mean daily rainfall for this sample is between 1.5 and 1.8 millimetres.
parts.solution_md:
The sample is large, so by the Central Limit theorem $\overline{X}$ is approximately normal with mean 1.6 and variance $\frac{σ^{2}}{n}$

`\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(1.6, \; \dfrac{0.6^{2}}{40}\right)`

**[B1 B1]**

![Normal curve for the sample mean with mean 1.6, with the area between 1.5 and 1.8 shaded](assets/059-normal-curve-for-the-sample-mean-with-mean-1-6-w.png)

Standardise each end using the formula for the sample mean, with $\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.6}{\sqrt{40}}$

$Z = \frac{\overline{X}-μ}{\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}}$

$\frac{1.5-1.6}{\frac{0.6}{\sqrt{40}}} = - 1 . 0540 \dots$

$\frac{1.8-1.6}{\frac{0.6}{\sqrt{40}}} = 2 . 1081 \dots$

**[M1]**

The required area is the area to the left of 2.108 minus the area to the left of −1.054. By symmetry, $Φ ( - 1 . 054 ) = 1 - Φ ( 1 . 054 )$

`\text{P}(1.5 < \bar{X} < 1.8) = \mathrm{\Phi}(2.108) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(1.054)\right)`

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 2.1 row and 0 column give 0.9821, and ADD 8 gives 3

$Φ ( 2 . 108 ) = 0 . 9821 + 0 . 0003 = 0 . 9824$

The 1.0 row and 5 column give 0.8531, and ADD 4 gives 9

$Φ ( 1 . 054 ) = 0 . 8531 + 0 . 0009 = 0 . 8540$

Substitute these values

$\text{P} ( 1 . 5 < \overline{X} < 1 . 8 ) = 0 . 9824 - ( 1 - 0 . 8540 ) = 0 . 8364$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 1 . 5 < \overline{X} < 1 . 8 ) = 0 . 836$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\overline{X}$ normal with mean 1.6, stated or used.
> 
> **B1**: Variance of $\overline{X}$ = $\frac{0.6^{2}}{40}$ (= 0.009), or standard deviation $\frac{0.6}{\sqrt{40}}$, stated or used.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising 1.5 or 1.8 with 1.6 and $\frac{0.6}{\sqrt{40}}$. The $\sqrt{40}$ must be present, and the standard deviation and variance must not be mixed.
> 
> **M1**: The correct area, consistent with the z-values found.
> 
> **A1**: 0.836 or 0.837, or answers which round to these.

parts.problem_md:
The gestation period, $X$ days, of female kangaroos of a certain species has a normal distribution with mean 29 and standard deviation 4.

Find the probability that the gestation period of a randomly chosen pregnant female kangaroo is between 27 and 30 days.
parts.solution_md:
![Normal curve for X with mean 29, with the area between 27 and 30 shaded](assets/060-normal-curve-for-x-with-mean-29-with-the-area-be.png)

Standardise each end using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

$\frac{27-29}{4} = - 0 . 5$

$\frac{30-29}{4} = 0 . 25$

**[M1]**

The required area is the area to the left of 0.25 minus the area to the left of −0.5. By symmetry, $Φ ( - 0 . 5 ) = 1 - Φ ( 0 . 5 )$

`\text{P}(27 < X < 30) = \mathrm{\Phi}(0.25) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(0.5)\right)`

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.2 row and 5 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 25 ) = 0 . 5987$

The 0.5 row and 0 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 5 ) = 0 . 6915$

Substitute these values

$\text{P} ( 27 < X < 30 ) = 0 . 5987 - ( 1 - 0 . 6915 ) = 0 . 2902$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 27 < X < 30 ) = 0 . 290$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising 27 or 30 with mean 29 and standard deviation 4. Using the variance 16 in place of 4 scores M0.
> 
> **M1**: The correct area, consistent with the z-values found, for example `\mathrm{\Phi}(0.25) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(0.5)\right)`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.290, or answers which round to 0.290.

parts.problem_md:
A random sample of 16 pregnant female kangaroos is chosen and the mean of their gestation periods is denoted by $\overline{X}$.

(i) State the distribution of $\overline{X}$, giving the values of any parameters.

(ii) Find $\text{P} ( 27 < \overline{X} < 30 )$.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

$X$ is normal, so $\overline{X}$ is normal with the same mean and variance $\frac{σ^{2}}{n}$

`\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(29, \; \dfrac{4^{2}}{16}\right)`

`\bar{X} \sim \text{N}(29, \; 1)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

![Normal curve for the sample mean with mean 29, with the area between 27 and 30 shaded](assets/061-normal-curve-for-the-sample-mean-with-mean-29-wi.png)

Standardise each end using the formula for the sample mean, with $\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{16}} = 1$

$Z = \frac{\overline{X}-μ}{\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}}$

$\frac{27-29}{1} = - 2$

$\frac{30-29}{1} = 1$

**[M1]**

As in part (a), use $Φ ( - 2 ) = 1 - Φ ( 2 )$

`\text{P}(27 < \bar{X} < 30) = \mathrm{\Phi}(1) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(2)\right)`

**[M1]**

The 1.0 row and 0 column give

$Φ ( 1 ) = 0 . 8413$

The 2.0 row and 0 column give

$Φ ( 2 ) = 0 . 9772$

Substitute these values

$\text{P} ( 27 < \overline{X} < 30 ) = 0 . 8413 - ( 1 - 0 . 9772 ) = 0 . 8185$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 27 < \overline{X} < 30 ) = 0 . 819$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: `\bar{X} \sim \text{N}(29, \; 1)`, or normal with mean 29 and variance 1. Accept standard deviation 1 if clearly identified.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising 27 or 30 with mean 29 and $\frac{4}{\sqrt{16}}$. Dividing by 4, or by 16, scores M0.
> 
> **M1**: The correct area, consistent with the z-values found.
> 
> **A1**: 0.819, or answers which round to 0.819. Accept 0.8185.

parts.problem_md: State, with a reason, whether it was necessary to use the Central Limit theorem in your answer to part (b).
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **No, because the population of gestation periods is normally distributed**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: "No" together with the reason that the population (or the underlying distribution) is normal. Both are needed.

parts.problem_md:
A spinner has 5 sectors labelled 1 to 5. The spinner is spun 150 times and it lands on the number 3 on 131 occasions.

Calculate an approximate 92% confidence interval for $p$, the probability that the spinner lands on the number 3 on any spin.
parts.solution_md:
Find the sample proportion

`\hat{p} = \dfrac{131}{150} = 0.8733\ldots`

**[B1]**

For a 92% interval, each tail has area 0.04, so find $z$ with $Φ ( z ) = 0 . 96$. In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the nearest value below 0.96 is in the 1.7 row and 5 column

$Φ ( 1 . 75 ) = 0 . 9599$

Subtract to find how much more area is needed

$0 . 96 - 0 . 9599 = 0 . 0001$

In the 1.7 row, 1 is in the ADD 1 column, so the third decimal place is 1

$z = 1 . 751$

**[B1]**

The sample proportion is approximately normal with standard deviation $\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$, and $p$ is estimated by `\hat{p}`, so the end-points are `\hat{p} \pm z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}\left(1 - \hat{p}\right)}{n}}`

$\frac{131}{150} \pm 1 . 751 \sqrt{\frac{\frac{131}{150}\times\frac{19}{150}}{150}}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Lower limit} = 0 . 82578 \dots$

$\text{Upper limit} = 0 . 92088 \dots$

$0 . 826 < p < 0 . 921$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: `\hat{p} = \dfrac{131}{150}` or 0.873 seen.
> 
> **B1**: z = 1.751 seen. Accept 1.75 if nothing better is seen.
> 
> **M1**: An expression of the form `\hat{p} \pm z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}\left(1 - \hat{p}\right)}{150}}` using the value of `\hat{p}` found. Any z-value scores this mark, but it must be a z-value, not a probability.
> 
> **A1**: $0 . 826 < p < 0 . 921$, or answers which round to these. The answer must be an interval: accept "0.826 to 0.921" or (0.826, 0.921).

parts.problem_md: Calculate the width of the confidence interval, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_md:
Subtract the unrounded end-points from part (a)

$0 . 92088 \dots - 0 . 82578 \dots = 0 . 09510 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Width} = 0 . 0951$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 0.0951. Accept $2 \times 1 . 751 \sqrt{\frac{0.8733\times0.1267}{150}}$ evaluated. Subtracting the rounded end-points (0.921 − 0.826 = 0.095) does not give the answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problem_md: Explain why the method used in part (a) would not be suitable if the spinner had only been spun 15 times.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The interval uses a normal approximation to the distribution of the sample proportion, which needs a large sample**

**[B1]**

With 15 spins and a proportion of about 0.873, the expected number of spins not landing on 3 is very small

`15 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{131}{150}\right) = 1.9`

**Final answer:** **This is less than 5, so 15 spins is too small a sample for the normal approximation to be valid**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The method needs a large sample (it uses a normal approximation, or the Central Limit theorem). Accept "15 is too small a sample".
> 
> **B1**: A supporting reason with a number, for example `n\left(1 - \hat{p}\right) \approx 1.9 < 5`, or "15 is less than 30". A reason with no number does not score this mark.

parts.problem_md:
The times, $T$ seconds, of a random sample of 8 TV adverts on *Channel π* are as follows.

| 35 | 61 | 42 | 40 | 37 | 35 | 53 | 49 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Calculate unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance of $T$.
parts.solution_md:
Find the sum of the times and the sum of their squares

$\sum t = 35 + 61 + 42 + 40 + 37 + 35 + 53 + 49 = 352$

$\sum t^{2} = 35^{2} + 61^{2} + 42^{2} + 40^{2} + 37^{2} + 35^{2} + 53^{2} + 49^{2} = 16  114$

To find an unbiased estimate of the population mean, use $\overline{t} = \frac{\sumt}{n}$ with $n = 8$

$\overline{t} = \frac{352}{8}$

$\overline{t} = 44$

**[B1]**

To find an unbiased estimate of the population variance, use `s^{2} = \dfrac{1}{n - 1}\left(\sum t^{2} - \dfrac{\left(\sum t\right)^{2}}{n}\right)`

`s^{2} = \dfrac{1}{7}\left(16\,114 - \dfrac{352^{2}}{8}\right)`

**[M1]**

$s^{2} = \frac{626}{7} = 89 . 428 \dots$

**Final answer:** $s^{2} = 89 . 4$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Unbiased estimate of the mean = 44.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution into either form of the unbiased variance formula. This mark can be implied by a correct answer. Use of the biased variance, dividing by 8 instead of 7 (giving 78.25), scores M0 A0.
> 
> **A1**: Unbiased estimate of the variance = 89.4, or answers which round to 89.4. Accept $\frac{626}{7}$.

parts.problem_md:
It is known that $T$ is normally distributed with variance 81.

Use the sample in part (a) to calculate a 95% confidence interval for the population mean of $T$.
parts.solution_md:
For a 95% interval, 0.975 is in the table of critical values in the formula booklet

$z = 1 . 96$

**[B1]**

The sample mean has standard deviation $\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}$, so the end-points are $\overline{t} \pm z \times \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}$, with the known $σ = \sqrt{81} = 9$

$44 \pm 1 . 96 \times \frac{9}{\sqrt{8}}$

**[M1]**

$44 - 1 . 96 \times \frac{9}{\sqrt{8}} = 37 . 763 \dots$

$44 + 1 . 96 \times \frac{9}{\sqrt{8}} = 50 . 236 \dots$

$37 . 8 < μ < 50 . 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = 1.96 seen.
> 
> **M1**: An expression of the form $44 \pm z \times \frac{9}{\sqrt{8}}$. Any z-value scores this mark, but it must be a z-value, not a probability. One side of the interval is enough for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $37 . 8 < μ < 50 . 2$, or answers which round to these. The answer must be an interval: accept "37.8 to 50.2" or (37.8, 50.2). An interval using the estimate 89.4 in place of 81 does not score this mark.

parts.problem_md:
The masses, $m$ grams, of a random sample of 80 potatoes from a farm are summarised as follows.

$n = 80$

$\sum m = 17  764$

$\sum m^{2} = 4  103  225$

Calculate unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance of the masses of potatoes from the farm.
parts.solution_md:
To find an unbiased estimate of the population mean, use $\overline{m} = \frac{\summ}{n}$

$\overline{m} = \frac{17764}{80}$

$\overline{m} = 222 . 05$

**[B1]**

To find an unbiased estimate of the population variance, use `s^{2} = \dfrac{1}{n - 1}\left(\sum m^{2} - \dfrac{\left(\sum m\right)^{2}}{n}\right)`

`s^{2} = \dfrac{1}{79}\left(4\,103\,225 - \dfrac{17\,764^{2}}{80}\right)`

**[M1]**

$s^{2} = \frac{158728.8}{79} = 2009 . 22 \dots$

**Final answer:** $s^{2} = 2010$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Unbiased estimate of the mean = 222.05. Accept 222.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution into either form of the unbiased variance formula. This mark can be implied by a correct answer. Use of the biased variance, dividing by 80 instead of 79 (giving 1984), scores M0 A0.
> 
> **A1**: Unbiased estimate of the variance = 2010, or answers which round to 2010. Accept 2009.2 or $\frac{158728.8}{79}$.

parts.problem_md: Calculate a 90% confidence interval for the population mean mass.
parts.solution_md:
For a 90% interval, 0.95 is in the table of critical values in the formula booklet

$z = 1 . 645$

**[B1]**

The sample mean has standard deviation $\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}$, and the unknown $σ^{2}$ is estimated by $s^{2}$ from part (a), so the end-points are $\overline{m} \pm z \sqrt{\frac{s^{2}}{n}}$

$222 . 05 \pm 1 . 645 \sqrt{\frac{2009.22\dots}{80}}$

**[M1]**

$222 . 05 - 1 . 645 \sqrt{\frac{2009.22\dots}{80}} = 213 . 806 \dots$

$222 . 05 + 1 . 645 \sqrt{\frac{2009.22\dots}{80}} = 230 . 293 \dots$

**Final answer:** $214 < μ < 230$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = 1.645 seen.
> 
> **M1**: An expression of the form $222 . 05 \pm z \sqrt{\frac{2009.2}{80}}$, using the value of $s^{2}$ from part (a). Any z-value scores this mark, but it must be a z-value, not a probability. One side of the interval is enough for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $214 < μ < 230$, or answers which round to these. The answer must be an interval: accept "214 to 230" or (214, 230). Follow through from a biased variance in part (a) is allowed for this mark only.

parts.problem_md: Explain why it was necessary to use the Central Limit theorem in your answer to part (b).
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The distribution of the population of masses is not known, so the Central Limit theorem is needed for the sample mean to be approximately normal**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A statement that the population distribution is unknown or not known to be normal. Accept "the population may not be normal". The reason must refer to the population (or the underlying distribution), not to the sample.

parts.problem_md:
The time, $T$ minutes, taken by a gamer to complete the final level of a video game is normally distributed with mean 57.2 and standard deviation 5.

During a competition, gamers are randomly divided into teams of 9 and each gamer plays the final level. The mean time, $\overline{T}$ minutes, for each team is calculated. Prizes are awarded to the teams whose mean times are in the fastest 10% of mean times.

(i) State the distribution of $\overline{T}$, giving the values of any parameters.

(ii) Find the maximum mean time that would lead to a team winning a prize. Give your answer in minutes and whole seconds.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

$T$ is normal, so $\overline{T}$ is normal with the same mean and variance $\frac{σ^{2}}{n}$

`\bar{T} \sim \text{N}\left(57.2, \; \dfrac{5^{2}}{9}\right)`

`\bar{T} \sim \text{N}\left(57.2, \; \dfrac{25}{9}\right)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

The fastest 10% of mean times are in the lower tail, so the maximum winning time $t$ satisfies $\text{P} ( \overline{T} < t ) = 0 . 1$

![Normal curve for the team mean time with mean 57.2, with the lower tail of area 0.1 shaded to the left of t](assets/062-normal-curve-for-the-team-mean-time-with-mean-57.png)

0.9 is in the table of critical values in the formula booklet, with $z = 1 . 282$. The tail is on the left, so by symmetry

$z = - 1 . 282$

**[B1]**

Standardise $t$ using the formula for the sample mean, with $\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}$

$Z = \frac{\overline{T}-μ}{\frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}}$

$\frac{t-57.2}{\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}} = - 1 . 282$

**[M1]**

$t = 57 . 2 - 1 . 282 \times \frac{5}{3} = 55 . 0633 \dots$

Convert the decimal part to seconds

$0 . 0633 \dots \times 60 = 3 . 8$* seconds*

A mean of 55 minutes 4 seconds would be above the cut-off, so round down

**Final answer:** **55 minutes 3 seconds**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: `\bar{T} \sim \text{N}\left(57.2, \; \dfrac{25}{9}\right)`, or normal with mean 57.2 and variance 2.78. Accept `\text{N}\left(57.2, \; \left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^{2}\right)`.
> 
> **B1**: z = −1.282 seen. Accept 1.282 used with the correct sign in the equation.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising $t$ with 57.2 and $\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}$, equated to a z-value. Dividing by 5 instead of $\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}$ scores M0.
> 
> **A1**: 55 minutes 3 seconds. An answer of 55 minutes 4 seconds is above the cut-off, so it does not score this mark.
